property_summary: For any nonzero ether deposit via receive(), the reference contract always increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant requires depositsCount+1<depositsCount which is impossible, so its receive() reverts for any deposit and thus does not succeed for some fuzzed deposit value.

For any caller sending any nonzero ether to C via its receive() entrypoint, the reference contract always accepts the deposit and increments depositsCount by 1; the mutant's inverted comparison makes receive() revert for any deposit, so some fuzzed deposit will cause the mutant to fail this rule.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount sent to C's receive() entrypoint, the reference contract accepts the deposit and increments depositsCount by 1 (so a successful receive increases depositsCount), whereas the mutant's inverted require makes receive() always revert for such deposits, breaking this property for some inputs.

For any caller sending any nonzero ether amount to C via its receive() entrypoint, the reference contract will accept the deposit and increment depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's inverted require causes receive() to revert for such deposits, breaking this rule for some fuzzed amount and caller.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount sent to C via its receive() entrypoint, the reference contract accepts the deposit and increases depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant's inverted require causes receive() to revert (so the post-call depositsCount does not increase) for some inputs.

For any incoming payable call to receive(), the reference C guarantees that depositsCount does not overflow (i.e., depositsCount + 1 >= depositsCount) so the call either succeeds only when the increment is non-wrapping; removing the check allows a wrapped overflow increment to occur for some large fuzzed deposit value, violating that invariant.

For any single payable receive() invocation sending value V from any sender, the reference contract C guarantees depositsCount after the call is either previous + 1 when the addition does not overflow and the call succeeds, or the call reverts when the invariant would fail; the mutant increments unconditionally allowing a wrapped overflow so there exists a V that makes depositsCount differ (overflow) — the test fuzzes the sent value to find such a case.

For any single payable invocation of receive(), the reference contract either accepts the payment and increments depositsCount without wrapping (depositsCount + 1 >= depositsCount) or the call reverts; the mutant increments unconditionally allowing a wrapped overflow so there exist deposit amounts that make depositsCount wrap and differ — the test fuzzes the deposit amount to expose this.

For any single payable call to receive() from any sender and any sent ETH amount, the reference C guarantees that depositsCount either increases by exactly 1 and remains >= previous (no unchecked wrap) or the call reverts; the mutant unconditionally increments allowing the post-call depositsCount to be strictly less than the pre-call value (wrap-around) for some input, so there exists a fuzzed sent value that makes depositsCount after the call < before the call, which the reference never allows.

For any single payable call to receive(), the reference C guarantees depositsCount after the call is >= depositsCount before the call (i.e., it never decreases), while the mutant can make depositsCount wrap and become less than before for certain large deposit amounts.

For any single ETH transfer to C via its receive() from any sender with any positive value, the contract's public depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant that increments twice violates this by sometimes increasing by 2.

For any payable call to receive(), depositsCount is non-decreasing (it increases by 1 on each successful receive); the mutant decrements depositsCount, violating monotonic non-decrease for some inputs.

For any successful payable call to receive, depositsCount never decreases (it is non-decreasing); the mutant decrements depositsCount on a receive call so it can make depositsCount decrease for some input amounts and sender sequences.

On every successful receive() call, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that assigns zero breaks this for inputs where depositsCount_before != uint256(-1) (typical values).

For any caller and any incoming ETH amount, calling receive increases depositsCount to a value >= its previous value (non-decreasing); the mutant that resets depositsCount to zero can make depositsCount decrease for some inputs, violating this universal non-decrease property.

For any sender and any nonzero ETH value, after calling receive the contract's depositsCount is nonzero if it was previously nonzero (i.e., receive never clears a positive depositsCount to zero); the mutant that assigns depositsCount = 0 can reset a previously positive depositsCount to zero and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any ETH value, calling receive() preserves that depositsCount after the call is strictly greater than or equal to the prior depositsCount (i.e., receive never decreases depositsCount); the mutant that sets depositsCount = 0 can make depositsCount decrease for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller and any incoming payable amount, invoking receive() on the correct contract leaves depositsCount equal to its previous value plus 1 (i.e., it increments by one); the mutant that assigns depositsCount = 0 breaks this because for some starting depositsCount values the post-call depositsCount will not equal previous + 1.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract callee used previously as a recipient of low-level calls, calling withdrawAll on the reference contract results in the contract's balance becoming zero (full balance forwarded to owner via withdraw), whereas the mutant that directly transfers to owner can leave the contract balance non-zero in the presence of a reentering/attacking recipient that manipulates state during withdrawAll — so the reference guarantees the contract balance is zero after withdrawAll for all inputs, the mutant can violate this for some inputs.

After any call to withdrawAll by the owner, the reference contract C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it sends entire balance via withdraw which uses transfer to msg.sender), whereas the mutant that directly transfers to owner can be disturbed by a reentrant recipient during the low-level transfer and leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any owner-triggered withdrawAll after the contract has a positive balance and an adversarial recipient is set as owner, the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it withdraws via withdraw which sends to msg.sender), while the mutant that transfers directly to owner can be interrupted by a reentrant owner/recipient and leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any owner calling withdrawAll after the contract holds some ETH and an external recipient (the owner) is a contract that reenters on receiving ETH, the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it routes through withdraw which sends to msg.sender), whereas the mutant that transfers directly to owner can be interrupted by a reentrant owner and leave address(c).balance > 0.

For every owner-invoked withdrawAll when the contract holds some ETH and the owner is a contract that reenters on receiving ETH, the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it routes through withdraw which performs transfer to msg.sender and is not vulnerable to the reentrancy ordering change), whereas the mutant that transfers directly to owner can be interrupted by a reentrant owner and leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the contract's entire ETH balance to the owner (so after the call address(c).balance == 0); the mutant no-op withdrawAll can leave a nonzero balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll causes the contract balance to become zero (reference); the mutant that makes withdrawAll a no-op can leave a nonzero balance for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance funded by the owner via receive(), calling withdrawAll causes the contract balance to become zero (reference); the mutant no-op withdrawAll can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance funded by ANY address, calling withdrawAll transfers the full contract balance out (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that makes withdrawAll a no-op can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance that was funded by sending ETH to the contract (via receive), after calling withdrawAll the reference contract always reduces address(c).balance to zero; the mutant that makes withdrawAll a no-op can leave a nonzero contract balance, so there exists some fuzzed funding amount and owner such that address(c).balance != 0 after calling withdrawAll on the mutant but is 0 on the reference.

Rule: Only the deployer (owner) can successfully call withdrawAll (i.e., when called by owner it always succeeds); the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners to call withdrawAll and thus makes calls by non-owners succeed while owner calls fail for some inputs.

For every caller address A, calling withdrawAll succeeds if and only if A == owner in the reference; the mutant inverts the ownership check so there exist callers for which the success boolean differs (non-owners may succeed and the owner may fail).

For any caller who is the owner and any withdraw amount <= contract balance, calling withdraw(uint) transfers that amount to the caller (so caller's external balance increases by that amount and contract balance decreases accordingly); the mutant that sends funds to the stored owner instead of msg.sender breaks this when the caller is the owner variable differs from msg.sender (i.e., a different owner account), causing the caller not to receive withdrawn funds.

For any caller address A and withdrawal amount v (where A is the contract owner set at deployment), a successful withdraw(v) sent by A must reduce the contract balance by v and result in address(A) receiving the funds; the mutant that sends funds to the stored owner instead of msg.sender will fail this when the caller (msg.sender) is not the stored owner, so the caller won't receive the withdrawn funds while the contract balance still decreases (or the stored owner receives them instead).

For any caller who is the contract owner at call time and any withdrawal amount not exceeding the contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) must result in the caller (msg.sender) being the recipient of the transferred Ether (the reference sends to msg.sender; the mutant sends to the stored owner address instead and thus can divert funds when msg.sender != owner).

For any caller address who is NOT the contract's stored owner and for any withdrawal amount <= contract balance, when that caller is made the owner via a prior action (i.e., msg.sender at construction differs from current caller), a successful withdraw(uint) must send Ether to msg.sender (the caller) — the mutant that sends to the stored owner instead will divert funds away from msg.sender when msg.sender != owner, so the reference preserves that caller's balance increase while the mutant does not.

For every caller address that is the current msg.sender invoking withdraw(uint) (and who is also the contract owner due to deployment), the reference always sends withdrawn Ether to msg.sender (so address(c).balance decreases by the withdrawn amount and msg.sender receives it); the mutant that sends to the stored owner instead breaks this when msg.sender != owner (i.e., when the caller is different from the stored owner), so there exists an input where the caller does not receive the funds while the reference would have sent them to msg.sender.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) after the contract holds at least amount wei, the reference forwards that amount out (contract balance decreases by amount), whereas the mutant that comments out the transfer leaves the contract balance unchanged for some amounts — the test fuzzes amount and owner to find such cases.

For any caller who is the owner and any nonzero withdraw amount not exceeding the contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) causes the contract balance to decrease by that amount in the correct contract; the mutant that comments out the transfer leaves the contract balance unchanged for some such inputs.

For any owner-initiated withdraw(amount) when the contract has >= amount balance, the correct contract transfers that amount out (address(c).balance decreases by amount) while the mutant that removes the transfer can leave the contract balance unchanged for some fuzzed amounts/owners.

For any owner calling withdraw(x) after the contract has at least x wei, the correct contract will reduce address(c).balance by exactly x (it forwards the funds); the mutant that comments out the transfer leaves the contract balance unchanged for some admissible inputs, so the invariant that balance decreases by x is broken by the mutant.

For every owner-invoked withdraw(amount) when the contract has at least amount wei, the reference contract forwards that amount out so address(c).balance decreases by exactly amount; the mutant that comments out the transfer can leave address(c).balance unchanged for some fuzzed amounts, violating this rule.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(x) after funding the contract with at least x wei, the reference contract transfers exactly x wei to the caller (so c.balance decreases by x); the mutant that always transfers 1 wei violates this for some x (e.g., x != 1).

For any caller funded as the owner and any withdraw amount x where the contract has at least x balance, calling withdraw(x) reduces address(c).balance by exactly x; the mutant that always transfers 1 wei breaks this when x != 1 (some inputs).

For any owner-triggered withdraw(x) where the contract has at least x balance, calling withdraw(x) reduces address(c).balance by exactly x; the mutant that always transfers 1 wei violates this for inputs x != 1 (some fuzzed x).

For any owner calling withdraw(x) when the contract has >= x balance, the amount actually sent to msg.sender equals the requested x (so address(c).balance decreases by x); the mutant that always transfers 1 wei breaks this when x != 1 — we express the property by observing that after withdraw, the contract balance equals its prior balance minus the requested x.

For any owner-triggered withdraw(uint256 amount) call when the contract has at least that amount, the reference decreases address(c).balance by exactly that amount; the mutant that always transfers 1 wei will not preserve that equality for many amounts (amounts != 1).

For any callee address that may revert when receiving funds, the reference C never reverts (it ignores callee failure) and thus calls to sendMoney always return successfully, whereas the mutant that requires call success will revert for some callee behaviors (e.g., a reverting fallback), breaking that property.
